CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 31st JANUARY, I860. þÿ þÿ We have now before us the discussions which took place in the Colonial Council on the 4th inst. relative to the Law of the Press. We take this opportunity to thank the honorable members who spoke in favor of the bill ; more especially the 1st member for this District, who, first and foremost in the advocacy of liberal measures, did not shrink from meeting the objections made against this most important one. His Excellency the Governor expressed himself in favor of the bill ; hut yet advanced some arguments against it, which, upon calm consideration, we doubt not that His Excellency would find to be equally against the liberty of the Press in most countries. That the cir-

$ & i Q) £ & Vj cumstance of the population of these Islands being of different creeds should be urged as a difficulty in the way of extending the law of the Press, appears to us to lie an objection of a very vague and unfounded nature; since, to admit its force, would be to close our eyes to the fact that, in those countries where the Press is most free, there we find the largest number of religious denominations. England and the United States furnish proof of our assertion : and in respect to objections urged on ihe ground of difference of races, viz : the and politi cal and social relations springing from Slavery, either existing or abolished, we think the latter country furnishes abundant proof that even these arc compatible with the freedom of the Press. We think that the force of the objection, made by His Excellency, in stating t hat society here has an existence of only 150 to 200 years, becomes lost when we bear in mind, that that state of society has not been grafted on the aboriginal Caribs, who, to the best of our knowledge, are totally extinct, but has been developed by Immigrants composed chiefly of Englishmen, Scotchmen, and Irishmen ; all coming from countries as civilized as the mothercountry. On this ground the age of society in these Islands cannot fairly he computed from the date of their colonization ; since, in doing so, we would altogether lose sight of this important fact. We come next to the argument based on the geographical position of these Islands, þÿ þÿplaced a , s His Excellency

says, þÿ between colonies with unlimited freedom on the one hand and colonies with slavery jon the þÿother. We must confess ourselves somewhat in'duuht as to the idea meant to he conveyed by His Excellency by Ihe expression þÿ unlimited þÿfreedom. His Excellency can, of course, not he supposed to mean that freedom in the British Colonies is unrestrained by laws, and punishments for their violation. Should the meaning of the expression therefore lie the right of an individual to act according to his free-will, consistently with the dictates of the laws of his country and society, we then must express our extreme regret to learn, from so high an authority, that that freedom does not exist here ; for we have always felt and exercised it, without being aware that it was peculiar to our English neighbours. About the same time that His Excellency uttered these words, there appeared an article in the London Times, which our readers will find in another part of our columns, in which that very freedom, characterized by His Excellency, as þÿ þÿunlimited, is held up to view as the source of prosperity to Engþÿland s Colonies. Even her West-India Colonies, though having passed through i the severe crises of Emancipation, and the subsequent free trade policy of the mother-country, ruinous as at first it was supposed to he, have still advanced, and are yet advancing to a state of prosperity unknown even in the flowery days of Slavery and Protection. Surely, when England, after confessing that she

has made every possible mistake in the art of colonization, points to a particular policy as the one which has best succeeded, her word ought to be believed ; for, if any modem nation has j had thorough experience in that art, that nation is the British.

THE UNITED STATES. Washington, Dec 30. The þÿPresident M s essage to Congress was delivered to the Country on the 27th Dec. The following is a synopsis : THE VIRGINIA TRAGEDY. The President, after expressing gratitude to the Almighty for blessings throughout the year, refers to the recent bloody occurrence at Harþÿper F s erry. These events, bad aud cruel in themselves, derived their chief importance from the apprehension that they are but symptoms of an incurable disease in the public mind, which may break out in still more dangerous outrages, and terminate at last, in open war by the North, to abolish slavery. While he himself entertained no such apprehensions, they ought to afford a solemn warning to us all to beware of the approach of danger Ho says : Lot me implore my countrymen, North of tivate their ancient feelings and South, t on inutuai forbearance and good will toward each other, and sh ire to allay the demon spirit of sectional i an and strife alive in the land. This advice proceeds from the heart of tie old public functionary, whose services commenced in the last generation, and the wise conservative statesman of that day ; but, he indulges in no gloomy forebodings He thinks the affair of þÿHarper Ferry s will be the means of allaying the existing excitement and preventing further outbreaks. SLAVERY IN THE TERRITORIES. He cordially congratulates Congress on the final settlement by the Supreme Court, of the question of Slavery in the territories.

The right has been established of every man to take his property, of every kind, including slaves, into the territories, which belongs equally to the whole Confederacy, and to have it protected there under the Federal Constitution. Neither Congress nor the Territorial Legislature, nor any human power has authority to annul or impair this vested light. Thus has the status of a territory during the intermediate period from its first settlement until it becomes a state, been irrevocably fixed by the final decision of the Supreme Court of the United States. ADMISSION OF NEW STATES. He then d' scribes the mode of admission of a territory as a State into the Union. It may be admitted with or without slavery as their constitution may prescribe. This principle has been recognized, in some form, by the almost unanimous vote of both houses of t ie last Congress. THE SLAVE TRADE. A'l lawful means at his command had !> r. employed and will continue to be employed, against the slave trade Our histoiy proves that the fathers of the Republic, in advance of all other nations, condemned the slave trade. THE CHINESE TREATY. Ratifications of the Chine e treaty have been exchanged. Two supplemental conventions are, however, pending, relating to the rights of Americans in China and transit duties. Ft >R EIG N RELATIONS. Our difficulty with Paraguay is satisfactorily adjusted. Our relations with Fiance, Russia, and all the continental governments of Europe, Spain perhaps, excepted, continue to be most

friendly. The President recommends that an appropriation bo made to meet the demands of the Amisted claimants. His opinions in favor of the acquisition of Cuba, by fair means, remain unchanged. Therefore, he again invites the serious attention of Congress to this important subject. (To be continued.,) o ENGLAND AND HER COLONIES.

In the recent torrent of abuse which lias been poured forth from so many vials on England and everything English, we have been over and over again reproached with the most greedy and boundless ambition, and with a lust for dominion which nothing short of the empire of the whole world car. satiate. Robbers on land, pirates on the deep; crushing all rival interests by monopoly, and, when the policy of monopoly is worn out, crushing all rival interests still more successfully by free trade ; plundering India,

seeking for a footing in China, first then deserting the West Indies, no object is þÿ exhausting too large for the ambition or too small for the cupidity of perfidious Albion. The same maw that has swallowed up the Empire of the Great i Mogul can condescend to make a meal on such petty dainties as Gibraltar, Malta, Corfu, and the singularly hard and dry morsel of Peritn. j It is in vain we protest that, if our censors have not outlived the illusions of territorial ambition, at any rate we have. Our censors do not believe in such moderation, probably because they feel incapable of it themselves, and cannot imagine how we can be proof to temptation which to them would be perlectly irresistible. When France is lavishing her millions of treasure and thousands of valuable lives to add to her dominions the poor and sandy wastes ol North Africa, or to subdue the fierce and blood-thirsty savages who crowd her possessions in the South Pacific; when Spain, after having lost during the present century the whole continent of South America, and no inconsiderable portion of the North, is seeking to indemnify herself by a raid on the barbarous hordes of Mauritania ; when Austria, with a baukvupt treasury and half-a dozen provinces on the point of rebellion, prefers to encounter the ruin which stares her in the face rather tliau abandon tire alien province of Venetia, the revenue of which is quite unequal to its extra military expense þÿ bow can France, | Spain, or Austria believe us when we tell them

that we are sick of territorial acqusitiou, that we would gladly diminish the limits of our sway, and that we hold our vast territories in a vety different spirit from that in which our ancestors acquired them ? Yet. we ought to he believed noihwitlist Hiding. We disclaim couqucst, uot from any particular disinterestedness, but because we have discovered a simpler, a surer, aud a more innocent way to national prosperity. We are the fortunate possessors of an ait of which, although we make no secret, no other nation has proved able to avail itself. We have shown that we can conquer, but so in its turn has every people in Europe, from Sweden in the north to Spain in the south. Hut that which we have done, and which no other uatiou since the days of ancient Greece has been able to do, is to plant colonics, to raiso up in distant lands communities which, secure under tire iegis of our power from invasion or insult, devote their whole energies to the arts of peace, and govern themselves by spontaneous choice, according to the laws and institutions ot the parent State. At a very small expense of money, and at no expense at all of blood, we have placed in the Noithern and Southern Temperate Zones numerous communities whose free commerce repays us a hundredfold the ex pauses of their foundation, whose broad lands offer an asylum to men whose enterprising spirit, is diseontenttd with the slow progress that can be made in an old and thickly-peopl d country, and whose successful settlers, returning home

with accumulated wealth, very perceptibly increase the riches of the mother country. Why should we ciuhark iu the uncertainties of war when vve can secure such peaceful yet glorious triumphs as these ? Well may as we we cent monopolies in trade so long discard all live to maintain the monopoly of the art of colonizing, which is better than the art of producing wealth, since ii is the art of planting communities who will produce it for us iu the shortest time, because under the most favourable circumstances. It is not difficult to sec what arc the conditions ot success in this pursuit, the possession of which has raised us so far above the competition of the other European Powers Having ourselves made every possible mistake in the art of colonization, we have gradually come to establish a number of rules by which wo guide our own opciatious, aud by which the operations ol have other European Power are guided. Wc no tried colonization both in tropical and temperate latitudes, and, having experience of both, we have come to the conclusion that the only colonies wc ought to plant for the future are those favourable in climate and position to the multiplication of our own race and the healthful diffusion of our own institutions. By overlooking this principle Holland, Spain, France, and Denmark have encumbered themselves with possessions which afford no permauent home for their European inhabitants, which are like our Indian Empire, a constant drain on their resources, a without possessing, like our Indian Empire,
vast semi-civilised population, whoso commerce

$ T« 0< S ft 11 1 ft V tl «. may reward them for the toils of Government. We have at last convinced ourselves that the best way to colouize is to make the colony an eligible place of residence for English men and women, and that not ouly as regards climate, but i laws, institutions, and habits. We have given to our colonies the means of making such laws j as please them, we have relieved them from all commercial restraints, and in great measure from the necessity of incurring expenditure for selfdefence. With the English money-market to draw on for loans, with the English army and navy to defend them from attack, they are placed in a positiou as h ippy aud as prosperous as ever fell to the lot of arty large number of the human race. We have given them, besides, perfect religious equality. What wouder, then, if our colonies have been able so far to outstrip communities nursed in the doctrines of monopoly, of centralizing interference, and of intellectual aud | Frederiksteds District þÿ religious subservience? As a signal instanc# of the success of this method ot colonization we may point to our Australian group of colonies, and more especially to that province which lias so far outstripped its neighbours and comp' titors, the noble colony of Victoria. It is now just 22 years since this colony was founded, and the first kaugaroo gave place to the inroad of the Hist civilized man. The balauce-sheet of the colony for the year 1858 is now lying before us. The receipts ror that year amount in round numbers to 3,000 00U?.,

the import duties alone amounting to 1,318,006?., the export duty on gold to 310,000?., the sales of public lands to 628 000?., the rent of public lands and licences of different trades to 331,000/., aud the postage to 89,000?. It seems absolutely incredible that such a fabric of prosperity can have been raised in such a shoit time by the entirely unaided exertions of a community a considerable portion of whom have been brought to their present position by a voyage nearly equaling in extent two-thirds of the diameter of the iihibc, without pecuniary assistance from tiic mother country, and with nothing hut their owu good sense and enetgy to guide them. It is indeed impossible to say how much more irosperous Victoria might have been It id England more rigorously abstained from interference with her consents, had she not by ill-advised meddling raised up within the colony a land monopoly, and checked the progress ot agricultural settlement by throwing difficulties in the way of the acquisition of the soil. This fatal legacy ot Imperial meddling still remains, and it is imbed wonderful to think what has been done in spite of so serious a drawback. This revenue has been raised by taxes imposed by the votes of a freely elected Assembly, and will be appropriated in like tnanuer. It is pretty nearly equal, if we mistake not, to the revenue extracted by the Papal Government from three millions and upwards of unfortunate subjects ; but no put of it is raised by a lottery, and no part of it is

wasted ou the disoideny police tni-named the Papal Army. We very much doubt, with all reverence be it spoken, whether the Pope would expend the money as well as the Assembly elected by the rude adventurers who have crowded to this remote corner of the world. 114,000?., for education, 24,000 ?., for scientific purposes, 25,000?., for sanitary improvements, 769,000?., for useful public works, 25.000?., towards the relief of sufferets by the Sepoy mutiny, 7,000? , for a public library, 000?,, 8 for an University purely- secular, and, above all, a cash balance of 458,000? , are items of Victorian expenditure which might well make infallibility blush, if infallibility had not long lost the habit. Leverrier, the discoverer of the planet ence of Academy of Sciences, between Neptune, Ims just announced the to exist- another planet Paris, Mercury the st ii I the Sun. In September last this distinguished astronomer communicated to the Academy an error in the motion of the perihelion of Mercury, which could only be explained on the assumption ofanother planet existing in the position indicated. It appears, however, that the new planet, prior to the announcement of M. Leverrier, had been discovered several months ago by a physician, Dr. Lescarhault, at Orgeres (Eureet- Loire). On the 26th of March last Dr Lescarhault took an observation of the Sun, and observed a small round black spot pass over th j þÿSun sdisc. This result he forwarded to M. Levcrrier, according to whose calculations the chord described by the planet must have subtended an arc of 9 minutes and 17 seconds, so that the doctor, with Ins primitive apparatus, was only four seconds wrong. The doctor estimates the diamelerof the new planet at 310 leagues, and the inclination of its orbit to the ecliptic at 12 degrees. If such are its dimensions, it is likely that there are more planets still in that region. Its revolution round the Sun is performed in 19 days and 17 hours; in its greatest elongations its distance trom the Sun does not exceed 7 degrees, while þÿMercury s maximum elongation is 25 degrees. Mr. Benjamin Scott, City Chamberlain, states that he saw the body alluded to in 1847, and that it was
seen by Mr. Lloft, an Englishman, in 1818. It is Mr. þÿScott s opinion that there are at least two planets between Mercury and the Sun.

DEI' 14de MODE holdtes Mandagen den 9de Januar. Raadet foretog : lste Behandling af Udkast otn Forandring i Skole-Regulationerne. Det 4de KongevalgteMedlem þÿ Ussing þÿ som Ordforer for Udvalget, udhaevede Majoritetens ledende Anskuelser, som freinsatte i Betaeukningen, der gaae ud paa: 1, at opnaae en Forbedring i Bornenes Underviisning, ved et Tilling afeet Aar til den lovbetalede Skolegangstid ; 2, en udvidet Virkekreds for Gouvernementet i mindre vigtige Anliggender istedetfor at der nu udfordres en Kongelig Sanction til blotte Detail-Spijrgsmual- 3, en Forandring i Skolernes Bestyrelse, der er aldeles i Hsenderne paa de maehriske Brodre. Det 3die kongevalgte Medlein þÿ Stakemaun þÿ dets Overveielse fern forskjellige yttrede, at der foreligger til Planer Raamed Hensyn til Tideu for Skolebesoget. 1, den gjeldende Anordning. som bestemmer 6 til 10 Aars Alderen for de fdrste 5 Dage i Ugen, med Ldverdagsskolcn for Born fra 10 til 13 Aar. 2, Committeens Minoritets - Betaenkning, som anbelaler Fastholdelsen af det bestaaende System. 2, Det af Gouverneuren forelagte Udkast, som foreslaaer SkolebesOg af alle Born mellem 6 og 13 Aar, fordeelte afvexlende over 3 Dage Ugen. i 4, Committeens Majoritets Betaenkning tilraadende en Forlaengelse af Skoletiden med eet Aar foruden den ved den gjeldende Anordning bestemte Periode, tilligemed en Afskaffelse af Loverdagsskolerne. 5, et Andragende fra endeel Individcr om en simpel Afskaffelse af Lciverdagsskolerne, saaledes at Tabet erstattes med en

Forogelse af Laererne. Den blotte Forskjelligartethed af de forelagte Planer giver allerede Grund til at betvivle, at der er nogen paatriengende Niidvendiglied at en Forlioldsregel, som ikke kail ivnerksaettes uden en Opoffrelse af det Arbeide, som udgjor en nOdvendig Betingelse for Oens Velviere. Indrdmmet at Bornene ikke liere saameget i Skolerne som er at onske, saa fblger deraf ikke, at Aarsagen alene er at tilskrive Kortheden af Tiden for SkolebesOget, og dersom Aursagen, hvilket ikke er usandsynligf, linger i Underviisnings-Methoden, vil en Forliengelse af Skoletiden ganske i sikkert en meget alvorlig Atgang Arbeidet, inedfore medens det er tvivlsomt, hvorvidt en tilsvarende Gevinst i Underviisningen vil opnaaes. Det er paastaaet af Committeens skolen Majoritet, at Indretningen med hos Loverdugs- befordrer Lediggang Bornene; Minoriteten megter dette, og Beviset mangier. Taleren niaatte i det hole bifalde Minoritetens Mening, at der ikke er fremkoinmen tiistrickkelige D.ita tor at forandre en Lov, som kun er udstapdt for 6 Aar siden efter mange og omhyggelige Undersogelser og Forhamllinger. Om det Onskelige af en storre Raadighed for den locale Bestyrelse at traffic mindre indgribende Foranstaltninger, ere Alle enige, men forinden man indlader sig i Sporgsmaalet om Unddragelse af Skolernes Ledelse og Overbestyrelse fra de maehriske Brodre, vilde det vaere nddvendigt at forvisse sig, om en saadan Forandring lader sig udfore uden at udkraeve fordgede Ud-
gifter,

Det lste Medlem for Trederiksteds District þÿ Sarauw þÿ henviste til de Motiver som ledsagede hans Forslag i sidste Session angaaende denne Sag for at vise paa hvilken Maade Ldverdagsskolerne belordre Lediggang. Gouverneuren forklarede Forholdet#med Landskolerne som en Overeenskomst mellem Hensyuet for Befolkningens nbdvendige Oplysning og den agerdyrkende Interesse. Skulde det Raadet forelagde Udkast ikke vinde Bifald, saa vilde han i Valget mellem Committeens to Betaenkninger give Minoritens Fortrinet, da han ikke antog at en Skoleunderviisning som kun varer til det fyldte llte Aar vilde fastholdes i Bornenes Sind. Han advarede mod de staerke Udtryk i Andragendet, som om Tabet af Bornenes Arbeide ved en Udvidelse af Skolegangen vilde gjiire det umuligt paa nogle Plantager at aftage Hosten, hvilket vil kunne misforstaaes som om et uforholdsmaessigt Qvautum Arbeide blev paalagt Bornene. Angaaende Loverdagsskolerne var det hans Mening, at de ere af meget liden Nytte, og han liar ofte fundet at Born som have besogt dem temmeligt regelmagssigt ere gaaede tilbage istedetfor frem fra den Tid de ophorte med den ordinaire Skolegang. Hvis den paataenkte Omskiftning af Skoledagene skulde medfore lor store Vanskeligheder, vilde et andet Arrangement maaskee kunne saettes istedet, ved at lade Bornene mellem 8 og 12 Aar gaae til Skolen i de nu gjeldende Skoletimer og dem fra 6 til 8 Aar besoge den i 2£ Time om Eftermiddagen; Bihjelperen vilde da kunne undvaeres og Plantagens Bud kun

vaere nodvendige for den yngere Afdeling af Bornene. Han vil ikke videre urgere paa de tvungne Besbg af Sondagsskolerne saaledes som optaget i Udkastet; og hvad angaaer St. Jan, vilde det vane rigtigst at lade Degnen overtage Skolelaerer-Forretningerne. Han billiger Forslaget om en udvidet Myndighed for Local-Regjeringen, og mener at den nuvaerende Overdragelse af liele Skolernes Overbestyrelse til de maehriske Brodres Samfund ikke er hvad der nicest kunde onskes, men foruden andre Puncter vil ogsaa Pengesporgsmaalet her blive at tage under Overveielse og deter tvivlsomt, om Forslaget at overdrage Skolebestyrelsen til Praesten for den danske Meniglied fortjener Anbefaling. Det lste Medlem for St. Jan þÿ Elliott þÿ udtalte sin Erkjendtlighed for den meget tilfredsstillende Maade, hvormed Gouverneuren i det forelagte Udkast er kommet de i Colonialraadets sidste Session udtalte Anskuelser irnode, men formeente, at Oens naervaerende Stilling er i hbiGrad ugunstig til Forandringer ; og da der nu er Grund til at vente en B'orbgelse af Arbeids-Befolkningen fra fremmede Steder, haaber han, at Omstaendighederne ville snart frembyde en Mulighed til Ivaarksaettelsen af Forholdsregler i den onskede Retning. Hvad angaaer den i Andragendet paaberoabte Umulighed at aftage Hosten, har han ingen Tvivl om at der denned taenkes paa Plantager paa Bakkerne, hvor Karrer ikke kunne bruges til Rorenes Transport og man traenger til Born for at drive de lsessede Muulaesler. Planternes Stilling

er saaledes, at de ikke kunne taale nogen Forringelse af den existerende Arbeidskraft, og hvad angaaer Skolernes Nytte, er det hans Mening at Bornene laere mere i Sdndagsskolen end i hele Ugen. Det 5te Medlem for Christiansteds District þÿ Rothe þÿ forklarede, at det Synspunkt som Committeens Minoritet har taget, er imod enhver Forandring. Den omhandlede Gjenstand ligner en Sag under Forligsinaegling, dog ikke mellem Skolens

og Planternes Iuteresse, men mellem Skolens og det Almindeliges Interesse, og denne sidste taaler iitgeti flere Opoffrelser. Faa Plantager have saa mange som 8 Muled rive re ; tages 3 af dem bort, ere de tilbagebiivende utilstra'kkelig til Arbeidet og Udgifterne til et 0|>syn. Ingeu kan , nsegte, at ved de gjeldemle Lovbestemmelser Skolerne ere, hvad Loven angaaer, satte paa en meget respectabel Fod. Den nugjeldende Periode af 10 Aar er allerede en | Concession i det omtalte Forliigsforliold, da Tiden oprindelig var 9 Aar men da selve 10 Aars Alderen blev betragtet som en vel ung Alder, bleve Lbverdagssko'erne foiede til som en Modvregt, og da denne sidste Forholdsregel valgtes var det ingenlunde overseet at den medforte et Offer for Forseldrenes Vedkommende ; men man fulgte den Grundsaetning, at et saadant Offer ikke allene var billigt men ogsaa gavnligt forsaavidt det var onskeligt, at Forte l (Irene skulde foie en Interesse i deres Borns Underviisning, og at denne Interesse vilde vtere ringere, hvis Underviisningen gaves uden noget Bidrag fra deres Side, da vi Alle kun stette ringe V;erdi paa hvad vi opnaae uden egen Anstnengelse. At Loverdags-Skolerne befinde sig i deres nuvterende utilfredsstillende Tilstand, er at tilskrive en Pligtforsommelse hos nogle blandt dem, hvem det paaligger at have Omsorg derfor, eller maaskee endog en forsaetlig Modvirken, endskjbndt fra i sig selv velmeente Hensyn. Det serede Medlem naegtede, at Loverdagsskolerne ere Aarsag til Lediggang, idet paa

mange Plantager intet Arbeide forrettes om Loverdagen paa en stor Deel af Aaret, og erklrerede Paastanden, at Skolebesoget om Loverdagen skulde virko til Hinder for Besdget af Sondagsskolerne for at vtere greben af Luften uden ringeste reel Grund. Loverdagsskolerne ere etablerede ved Love og som saadanne bor de opretholdes. Majoritetens Forslag vilde medfore en Fordgelse af 20 pCt. i Skolebornenes Antal, og nOdvendiggjore en tilsvarende Forogelse ei alene af Laerere men ogsaa af Skolebygninger og Beboelses-Leiligheder for Laerere. Forslaget at tvinge alle Born til deres fyldte 13de Aar at gaae 3 Dage om Ugen i Skolen vil ganske sikkert forvolde Utilfredshed ogsaa blandt Foneldrene, Born imellem 10 og 13 Aar kunne nu altid i Hosttiden tjene deres 5 Quanters Meel og 5 gamle Realer om Ugen, og at betage dem eller formindske denne Fortjeneste vil opvaekke mereMisfornoielse end Loverdagsskolerne gjore. From llie London Times It is now announced almost in official language that England and France have tally agreed to recognize and protect the Central Italian State which has been formed oat of the Duchies of Tuscan v. Parma, and Modena, and the Papal province of the Romagna. This consummation lias been for some time certain, and wo were enabled to allude to it as soon ns the refusal of the Catholic Powers to join in the Congicss made it no longer necessary to consult them in the matter However, the policy of England is so evidently to avoid all active interference in Ita'y that our Government has wisely allowed the French Emperor to take the initiative in all that has been done, and if we have any band in settling the future destinies of Italy it will only he as the counsellors of the great Power which lies on her borders, and whose army still occupii s Rome aud Lombardy. The part which this country has played in the Italian question is so worthy of our character and our high plaeo in Europe that it may not be amiss to glance over the principal cveuts which have marked the history of the last six months. That a nation which steadfastly resolves to keep aloof from a great struggle, and which consequently receives the vituperation of every party to the dispute, should in the course of halt a year succeed in impressing its policy on all concerned, and should stand forth as the friend, counsellor, and protector of the Italian people, is certainly a triump to the principle of non-interference, aod is calculated to encourage the country in that
course of dignified isolation from continental broils which has been inaugurated in the past year.

The French Emperor, intent for the time on military glory, seems to have felt that the victory of Solferrno had secured his throne. What was there to be gained by the war more than the complete overthrow of an Austrian army ? and this had been accomplished in the most extended battle fought since the day ofLeipsic. From the evening of Solferiuo, therefore, the French Emperor was ready to conclude peace. The state of Europe was such as to confirm him in this resolution. England, though determined not to interfere, was known to be averse from any disturbance of the peace of Europe. Prussia aod the minor German States had armed, the fortresses of the Confederation were strengthened, all the military establishments put on a war footing, and Bavaria had committed almost an act of war by forwarding Austrian troops and stores through her territory. Then there was the famous Quadrilateral, which would require a siege or a succession of sieges, beginning in tire hottest months of an excessively sultry year. We can hardly wonder, then, that Napoleon 111., satiated with military glory, and perhaps nut unwilling to continue the traditions of the fiist þÿBonaparte tenderness s for Austria, should have given the Austrian Emperor easy terms at Villalranca. But, in truth, the astuteness of the young autocrat seems to have got t lie better of his more experienced opponent. Francis Joseph gained almost all be, wanted, and more than he could reasonably have expected, while the French Emperor, led away by visions of a f ederal

Italy, with the Pope at its head, and Austria as a docile member, gave up what the world thought to he the natural fruits of his victory. One thing is perfectly clear, þÿ that Napoleon was in no way prepared for the reception which his arrangement met with from Europe. From Italy rose a cry ol anger and shame. In every free press indignation and ridicule were mingled with incredulity. In Frauce itself the news was received with a blank silence, even more expressive than the demonstrations ot the Piedmontese or the exultation of the German Courts. Of course, it was impossible for the Emperor to re- j nounce the promises which lie had made, and on which it might be said that Austria had ceded Lombardy to his ally. Then his pride forbade that he should own himself outwitted, or that he should seem to repent of the arrangement to which he was pledged Accordingly, the more Europe sneered or Italy complained, the more the Emperor persisted in upholding the terms of tiie convention. In order that it might seem there was in his opinion, nothing to regret, lie ticatid the Austrians with a cordiality which Verged on obsequiousness, and distinguished Priuce Mctteruich as if he had been the representative of an old and trusted ally The whole hearing of the Imperial Court too much resembled its conduct after the conclusion of the peace with llus-ia. In the meantime the journals opposed to this country had their way, and t hose tirades were published which roused in the English people a spirit of which the Volun-

teer movement is the result. But the indignation of Italy and the remonstrances of this country were not to be quieted by any concert between the lately hostile Courts. The people of Central Italy held their own ; ill spite of per-

receive back their fugitive Sovereigns, and the King of Sardinia, though compelled to temporize, was yet sufficiently independent, to exercise an act of sovereignty, by allowing M. Buoncompagui to accept the functions of Regent. In the meantime, it became necessary, in the French þÿEmperor opinion, s to call together tile nations of Europe, in order to decido ott the futuce settlement ot Italy. What were the real views of Napoleon and Count Walewski wo cannot say ; but it is plain that the refusal of our Government to take any part in the Congiess unless the liberties of Control Italy weic secured from armed invasion had no small effect in the councils of the Tuileries From that time the Emperor felt that he must break cither with the tree States of Europe and the enlightened opinion of his own country, or with the Emperor of Austria and the Roman priesthood. He could not hope to find a middle course. The Italians, relying on the moral support of the friends of liborty in both hemispheres, would make no unworthy concession. Austria and the Pope were pressing for an armed interference to carryout the Treaty Zurich, of while England, true to her high mission, had declared that no such act should have her concurrence. The struggle has been a long one, but it is

$ TV g KQ) G 1 A VI now over. The French Emperor has taken his course, and it is one which will help to reconcile him with that great body of liberal-minded and reflecting men who have watched with anxiety and regret his recent policy. lie has resolved to show to the world that he did not make war for empty glory or to strengthen a tottering throne, or to employ a dangerous army, but to give to a gifted and unfortunate people that freedom which has been so long denied them. The concert which has thus been established between France and England is the guarantee for the freedom of Italy. We believe that the mere fact of such an understanding subsisting will be enough to settle all the questions now in dispute. It is reported that when the French Emperor determined on adopting the policy recommended by England he applied to our Government to know whether we were willing to stand by him should Austria seek to enforce the Treaty of Zurich by another appeal to arms. It. would have been, in any case, a departure from our established policy to enter iuto such an engagement, but happily the thing was not necessary To the inquiries of the British Government Austria is said to have answered that she had neither the will nor the power to enter into another Italian campaign, and that if France resisted the restoration ol the legitimate rulers in Italy, Austria could only protest against the injustice. To France now belongs the settlement of Central Italy. England will still hold to her principle of avoiding actual interference,

though, no doubt, the two countries will join in a common plan for recognizing and assisting t lie new Government. We may congratulate our countrymen and the world that the year opens so auspiciously, and hope that the Italian people are now at the dawn of a long day of prosperity. o The Order of the Elephant. þÿ The fire which consumed the Royal Palace of Fredericksborg, in Denmark, a few days ago, also caused the destruction of various inestimable museums of natural history and antiquity. But there are other losses also to deplore, and among them the whole collection of the armorial devices of the Knights of the Elephant, from its first foundation down to the present time. The Order of the Elephant is, next to those of the Garter and of the Golden Fleece, the oldest in Europe, having been founded by Christian 1., King of Denmark, about the beginning of the loth century ; although others assign an earlier date to it, maintaining that it had been founded in commemoration of a noble Dane who had killed an elephant during one of the crusades in Palestine. As the Order was a religious one, the Knights swearing to defend the faith, its statutes were confirmed by Papal bulls in 14G2, the Popes never missing an opportunity of imposing their authority, whether wanted or nut; and the Catholicity oftheord r was further confirmed by attaching the image of the Virgin to the emblematic chain, the links suasion, and almost threats, they declined to | of which are, to this day alternately

elephants and small towers. Of course, when Protestantism was definitely established in Denmark all this was changed ; the image of the Virgin was suppressed, and all the Knights bound to follow the Lutheran Creed. At present the insignia of the Order consist ot an elephant of white enamel, with gold tusks and a blue housing, on which rises a tower; a negro holding a elephant. golden arrow is seated on þÿ The inotto is, the neck of the Pretimn magþÿnanimi. The Order, as regards Danish subjects at least, is only conferred on those who are already decorated with the Danebrog of the second class; and if they do not belong to the latter order, they receive it eight days beforehand, but are obliged to divest themselves of it immediately on receiving that of the Elephant, which cannot be worn with any other. Every newly-created Knight was, before the late disaster, obliged to send his coat of arms to the Palace of Fredericksborg. The 1st of January is considered the anniversary of the Order. þÿ London Paper.

The Astronomy of the Ancients. þÿ Professor Mitchell, in his lecture on astronomy, related a very remarkable fact, lie said that he had not long since met in the city of St. Louis, Missouri, a man of great scientific attainments, who for 40 years had been engaged in Egypt deciphering the hieroglyphics of the ancients. This gentleman had stated to him that he had lately unravelled the inscription upon the coffin of a mummy, now in the British Museum, and that by the aid of previous observation he had discovered the key to all the astronomical knowledge of the Egyptians. The zodiac, with the exact positions of the planets, was delineated on the coffin, and the date to which they pointed was the autumnal equinox in the year 1722 before Christ, or nearly .3,600 years ago. Professor Mitchell employed his assistants to ascertain the exact position of the heavenly bodies belonging to our solar system on the equinox of that year (1722 b. c.), and send him a correct diagram of them, without having communicated his object in doing so. In compliance with this the calculations were made, and to his astonishment, on comparing the result with the statements of his scientific friend already referred to, it was found that, on the 7th of October, 1722 b. c., the moon and planets had occupied the exact positions in the heavens marked upon the coffin in the British Museum. þÿ Ibid.

The Session of the British Parliament was opened on the 24th January by the Queen in person. In relation to Italian affairs hir Majesty observed : þÿ At the close of the last Session I informed you that overtures had been made to me to ascertain whether, if a Conference should be held by the Great Powers of Europe, for the purpose of settling arrangements connected with the present state and future condition of Italy, a Plenipotentiary would be sent by me to assi:t at such a Conference. I have since received a formal invitation front the Emperor of Austria and front the Emperor of the French to send a Plenipotentiary to a Congress to consist of the representatives of the eight Powers who weie parties to the Treaties of Vienua of 1815, the objects of such Congress being stated to be to receive communication of the Tieaties concluded at Zurich ; and to deliberate, associating with the above-mentioned Powers the Courts of Rome, of Sardinia, and of the Two Sicilies, on the means best adapted for the pacification of Italy, and for placing its prosperity on a solid and durable basis. Desirous, at all times, to concur in proceedings having for their object the maintenance of peace, 1 accepted the iuvitation, but, at the same time, I made known that, in such a Congress, 1 should steadfastly maintain the principle that no external lorec should be employed to impose upon the people of Italy any particu-

lar Government or Constitution. Circumstances have arisen which have led to a postponement of the Congress, without any day having been fixed for its meeting ; but, whether in Congress or in separate negotiation, 1 shall endeavor to obtain for the people of Italy freedom from foreign interference by force of arms in their internal concerns, and I trust that the affairs of the Italian Peninsula may be peacefully and satisfactorily þÿsettled. THE made use of as a quarantine estab- Protestant Quay being at present lishment for certain persons landed from a vessel recently arrived in this harbour, one of which persons is infected with small-pox, and the rest are to be kept under Surveillance, every one with exception of the olbeers and functionaries belonging to the quarantine-department and their attendants in the quarantineboats, is hereby forbidden to go to or to land at the Protestant Quay. In like manner the persons at present on the Quay are forbidden to leave it themselves or to let clothes or other effects be removed from there without special permission of the quarantine-authorities, and even then in any other than the quarantine boats. According to the Ordinance on the subject of quarantine dated 8th February 1805 infringement of the quarantineregulations are visited with capital punishment, and whoever may attempt to break through them, will have to blame himself for whatever injury he may suffer to life or limbs by shot or otherwise. NEWS If ISO HI WASHINGTON. WASHINGTON, March 8, 1860. The Treaty with Mexico. The fiiends of the Mexican treaty are now satisfied that the opinion repeatedly expressed in this correspondence, that it cannot be ratified, is a fact. They give it up. All sorts of threats have been made that a failure to ratify it would involve the two countries in a war, while the principal point of objection to its ratification by the republican Senators has been, tliat. to ratify it would be recognizing a tnob at Vera Cruz, and not a constitutional government representing the people of Mexico, which would inevitably involve the United States in 3 war with the church party to sustain the mob. The main question has been a constitutional one in the minds of the republicans, which precluded them from considering the details of the treaty commercially to any extent. The commercial advantages, so far as they have been discussed, have not been deemed of importance. The ratification would confer upon certain speculators, official and otherwise, a magnificent railroad job. The prevailing opinion is that the movements of the general government, to sustain Governor Houston in his Texas expeditioir against the Mexicans will result in a war between Mexico and the United States, so that, the seekers of a war with that pnny republie will be gratified without ratifying the treaty. But the hungry claimants who have been working here for weeks to grab two millions of the public money are sadly disappointed, and will have to borrow to get home. Senators Mason and Toombs, in conversation

with the President and Secretary of State today, in regard to Mexican affairs, stated that they saw no hope for the ratification of the Mexican treaty, and that they looked upon it as virtually dead. What course the administration will adopt in regard to Mexican affairs has not been determined upon They have all along labored under the impression that the treaty would eventually be ratified. Mr. McLane will sail in the Biooklyn frofn New York on Saturday for Vera Cruz. The government think it highly important, in the present condition of affairs, that our Minister should he constantly in the vicinity of Vera Cruz, to giun d and protect our interests. Some newspapers have eironeously staled that the Home squadron's movements will he governed in a great degree by his directions. The truth is, the flag-captain receives his ordeis from the Navy Department, but may be requested to avail himself of frequent consultations with our Minister, which, it is supposed in prominent quarters, lie will cl eerfully do. Mr. McLane's leiurn is with reference to the protection of Amciiean persons and property. THE DISPUTE BETWEEN 'I ME BANKERS AND MR. From the London Times, Feb. 28. THE ITALIAN QUESTION. To-night, unless Her þÿMajesty s Government should again interpose, the House of Commons will have to discuss ttie present phase of the proposal for annexing Savoy and Nice to the empire of France. Mr. Monckton Millies intends to meet Mr. þÿKinglake motion s l>v þÿ the previous þÿquestion, and it will not he difficult to find a plausible objection to the employment of the time of the House upon so vague and transitory and ever-changing a figment as this, which has from day to day been dangled in the public view. Time was when we were all accustomed to regard the Emperor of the French its a stern, mysterious man, whose designs had been burnt in upon his mind, and whose course of action was never varied hy t lie circumstances with which he was surrounded. When he retired from a position he had taken, the world was ready to believe that he hud gone hack only to gather impetus for a forward leap. Recent experience, however, Ims a little qualified this conviction. We can understand that a man should patiently make his way hy a series of tacks against ail adverse wind; hut we do not altogether recognize a man of strong purpose in the sailor who hears away every time the wind shifts tor the port immediately under his lee. We have seen so many changes come over the spirit of this dream of Italian unity, that the attention grows weary as we follow the apparently infinite and eventless varieties of form through which it passes. Lookers-on are beginning to think that the great

reconstructor of the map of Europe is less like a man who knows his geography than like a hoy with a puzzle map trying at haphazard one piece against another, and trusting chance to help him to a possible combination. A few days since everything appeared to he settled. The Pope was to he left in the enjoyment of all the glory of martyrdom, and Europe was to look on and see his imbecile tyranny subside. Tuscany, and the Romagna, and the Duchies were to he allowed to gravitate towards Piedmont; and the only remaining doubt was, whether France would seek her own advantage by seizing upon the Duchy of Savoy and the County of Nice. While we were looking upon this view, lo! the colours grew faint, and, as they faded away, other lineaments appeared upon the illuminated disc. Now we have altogether a new scheme. What has happened to produce this revolution in French counsels we are not told. Whether it he that France has become convinced of the warlike character of

the Italian nation, and grown apprehen sive of so enterprising and ambitious a monarchy; whether that timorous and defenceless French nation has awakened to the danger of lying side by side with those fierce Italians, and has discovered that no possession of Alpine passes can , give security against such a foe; þÿ whether these or other equally powerful j reasons have worked the change vve have not been told; but the whole question is again thrown into chaos, and we are again set to tr) new combinations. All Italy lias been long waiting for some ! declaration of what its destiny is to he. The oracle, however, cannot make up its own mind. A word of permission would have fixed all the States of Italy in one coherent mass, and ever and t anon that word has been half spoken and hastily retracted. We are astonished at such shifting counsels where we had been accustomed to such prompt resolves. Does our great allv doubt the sincerity of þÿAustria expressions s of humiliation þÿ does he dread that her attit .de of sufferance is only a pretence, and that he may have to fight another Solferino if he make himself the protector of a Unite. I Italy? Or is that early notion of a kingdom of Etruria recurring to his mind? No one can tell All we are allowed to know is, that while the Italians are impatiently awaiting t lie permission to unite, another and an entirely different scheme is sent down to amuse or to distract them. It is now suggested that Tuscany, instead of being annexed to Pied-

mont, shall remain the small powerless principality which it was when Napoleon III. crossed the Alps, and that the Romagna shall go hack to the suzerainty of the Pope under the Government of a Grand Vicar. As Tuscany will not ieeeive back her Grand Duke, it is proposed that stie shall accept as a substitute a child six years old, the nephew of the King of Sardinia, who shall govern hy a Regent. This is to undo all things, and to return again to Villafranca and Zurich. It is the re'mposition of a state of disniemliet ment ; it is the perpetuation of a state of insecurity, which leaves every possibility open for the return of the Austrian þÿ .Archdukes. How such a proposal will he received hy the people who have been, daily expecting the full fruition of thenlong deterred hopes it is not difficult to anticipate. Amid all these shilling counsels and irresolute schemings the purpose of tlie Italians has never varied, and their enthusiasm has never slackened- No ill management in the governing powers at þÿ Turinhas ever been able to shake their persistence in the determination to unite themselves with the only Italian Monarchy which offers itself as a nucleus for a great It alian State. They have been tested, and tried, and wearied, and disgusted in vain. Their idols have been taken from them; the Generals and Statesmen in whom they chiefly trusted have been removed; hut their tenacity of purpose has carried them through every trial, and has made their loyally to the King of their

adoption a faith. When Victor Emmanuel went to Milan the other day it was imagined that some recent events might have lessened the cordiality of his reception. All these expectations were disappointed. No crowned head in the world would any where he received with the assiduous and importunate homage with which the Lombards were incessant in their pains to prove that their affection for their King and their cause

was unabated. Does any one suppose | that the enthusiasm will be less w1 .mi Victor Emmanuel goes to Florence, or that the cheers will flag when be enters Boloirna ? ll is too late now to propitiate the i Dope and to draw near to Austria. If ever there was a time when it Was pruden' to grasp the nettle danger in order to pluck the flower safely, it is now, when the Emperor of the French has done enough to forfeit the confidence of the Papal hierarchy, and has not done enough to frighten it into submission, lie may depend upon it that, do what he may, Pio Norm will never again look on him as the eldest son of the Church, upon whom she may rely in any straits to which her tyranny or her arrogance may bring her. Meantime events are marching onwards, and are gathering an impetus which would require all the strength of even his powerful arm to arrest In a few days the Deputies from Central Italy and the Romagna will assemble at Turin, and will vote tile annexation of their respective States to Piedmont. They will he acting upon the implied sanction of all the great Powers of Europe. England lias openly approved, France lias q life as openly intimated her consent, Russia has assented with a gentle protest, and Austria It s declared that she will oiler no direct opposition. If the Deputies are well advised, they will act promptly upon this universal sanction; and, it Victor Emmanuel he equal to his great opportunity, he will at once assume the Crown which the populations offer him,

and which Europe has assented to his accepting. Can it lie possible that, alter all has been done, Napoleon III., the Liberator ot Italy, will go armed into the Assembly and forbid the great coiisYiinmation ol his own work? Tins would indeed he to settle all question ot the annexation of Savoy, and to render its discussion ridiculous. If there is to be no great Italian kingdom, there ran he no pretence for strengthening the frontier line of France. To seize upon the territory of Piedmont under such circumstances would he unilisscmhled robbery. The common consciem e ot Europe would not endure it, and we eamiot think that the Emperor ol the French is capable of imagining it. Perhaps lie intends to forego all thoughts of that new French province, to how before the hostile powers of the Church, and to speak softly again to Austria? Perhaps he may he onlv raiding a difficulty in order that he may ask Savoy and Nice as the price of removing it? Perhaps lie may have no very determinate resolution about the matter? The wind hloweth where it listeth, hut who shall say whence it coineth or whither it goelli ?

Enter Servant. Jack (says he) I have heard you are a great Gamester. Jack. My Lord, I should be glad to know who informed you thus; for 1 am sure the Report is false. blaster. Jack. 1 am sorry, my Lord, you are thus informed ; for so far from being a Card player, that as to the common Use of them I scarce know what it means Master. I will call the Informer, that I may know whether it be true or false. Enter Informer. Did you not tell me that Jack was a great Gamester at Cards. Informer. Yes, I did, my Lord, and he certainly is as great a Gamester as any in England. þÿ If you will take tbe Trouble of searching him you will find a Pack of Cards about him, for lie is never without. living searched they were found. Publication. HE Protestant Quay being at present made use of as a quarantine establishment for certain persons landed from a vessel recently arrived in this harbour, one of which persons is infected with small-pox, and the rest are to be kept under Surveillance, every one with exception of the officers and functionaries belonging to the quarantine-department i and their attendants in the quarantineboats, is hereby forbidden to go to or to i land at the Protestant Quay. In like manner the persons at present on the Quay are forbidden to leave it themselves or to let clothes or other effects be removed from there without special permission of the quarantine-authorities, and even then in any other than the quarantine boats. According to the Ordinance on the subject ary 1805 of infringement quarantine of the dated quarantine- 8th Februregulations are whoever ishment, and visited with capital pun- may attempt to break through them, will have to blame himself for whatever injury he may suffer to life or limbs by shot or otherwise. In conformity with the above orders have been issued to the fort and military posts to prevent the forbidden communication to or from the Protestant Quay. This is brought to the public notice by Order of the Governor. Christiansteds Police Office, 26th March I860. J. A. STAKEMANN.

OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL. Fourth Sessioa. THE 18th MEETING was held on Thursday the 2nd February at 11 o'clock, when the Council continued the discussion on the draft of a budget. The 5th member for Christiansted, Rothe, stated, that in consequence of the Governor's remarks on the double export-duty the Committee would advise the Council in its final Report to petition for a Royal provisional Ordiuance on this subject, as well as with regard to the duties on the produce of St. Johns. d, & e, No. 1. The Governor stated iu opposition to the Remarks iu the Report as if the $350 contributed yearly by the State-Treasury for the school at St. Johns cannot be looked upon as an advance, that the item had from the very beginning, and after being discussed in the Colonial Council been granted as an advance. Properly speaking the amount ought to be left out altogether and be paid by the Country Treasury of St. Johns, and if the recommendation of this Council to remit the whole of the debt to the State-Treasury be acted upon, the island will be able to defray the expense. c. 2. The Governor admitted, that the expenditure of the military establishment is very high, and if the arrangements could be limited to the immediate requirements of tne actual service, a smaller number of in n would be sufficient, but when the circumstances of the case are considered, among other tilings, that the enlistment must take place iu Europe, it will be seen that there must always to a certain extent be provided a larger number. The amount at which the expenditure is estimated

is too high, even the sum of $115,000 posted in the draft includes an amount of $3000, which may be looked upon as incidental tor the financial year to which the draft refers, arising from the circumstauce that certain expenses connected with the enlistment for two years happen to fall upon the budget of one year, the corresponding amount, not appearing in the budget of the year, for which it lias strictly speaking been applied, and the expenses on military buildings, which in the Report is put down that $10,000 falls in reality greatly short of at amount. In order to effect a saving in this branch, the number of the soldiers has been kept about 100 below the but number, on in the plan of 1851, on account of the determined rise of prices on all articles of consumption, even of clothing, the sum s aved lias not exceeded $8000. Admitting that the cost of the military establishment stands in a very high proportion to the whole expenditure, it must not be overlooked, that several other services, which by their nature are not military are performed by soldiers at considerable less expense, than would otherwise have to be incurred. In judging of the amount, of force required. it is also to be considered, that it is to

% f « © ® ® D X k V?3 8« be p op irtioned so as not only to put down violence, but to preclude every temptation to violent resis ance against the laws. We must also wli n we speak of the peaceable disposition of the population remember the excitable nature of a part of that population, the mutinous conduct evinced iu some of the neighbouring countries on the most frivolous motives, and the loose bonds of society in others. The measure of withdrawing all military force could be ad ipted by the British Government which lus resou ees especially in its naval station, which are not ar our disposal. He must also mention, that a petition lias been forwarded to hi in from almost all the planters and merchants in Frederiksted, recommending an augmentation rather than a reduction of the military force. He protested against the responsibility which the proposed reduction of $25,000 and a corresponding diminution of the military number throw upon the Government. The would forming the basis of the general sketch of a plan in the Report is but, very little less thau that at which the force lias been actually kept during the last years. Ilis Excellency then passed the particulars of the prop >sa! order Report of the Committee in review in in the to prove their incorrectness and inexpediency. His own calculations proceeding on the arrangements proposed by the Committee show only a saving of $6000 and the difference between that sum and the $25,000 of the Committee is owing to tie Committee having started from

the position that the number of the military is actually 480 which is not the case. He thinks that a saving may be effected by abolishing the maintenance of the garrison of Frederikst-d as a company, and making it again a simple detachment as was the case before 1848. The information recently received front nte respecting the intended policy of this Government in the Savoy question is thus confirmed hy a semi-official correspondent of the Augsburg Gazette : " Vienna, March 8. "Very many conjectures, almost all of which tire devoid ot' foundation, have been made on the subject of the policy of Austria in the Savoy question. Until now Austria has given no official declaration on the subject in question, but entertained the opinion it is known that she shares hy Russia and Prussia, that the aggrandizement of France hy means of Savoy and Nice would form a dangerous precedent. From Valparaiso to Copiapo and Tres Puntos, a railway is already constructed, chiefly for mining purposes, to an elevation of six thousand f et ; and as the Pass proposed for the line is not choked with snow in wiuler, and the whole distance is not moro than eleven hundred miles, the possibility of the scheme is believed in. þÿ A river, heretofore unknown, has been discovered in Vancouver's

This will bo good news for emigrants and settleis, especially as there is now a prospect of a fair and friendly settlement of the boundary þÿdispute. Tuscany has at last set about reclaiming one of the large marches which render her soil unfertile and unhealthy : it. comprises 1300 acres in the province of Pisa, and if the work is a beginning in earnest with the many similaily needful reclamations that have been neglected for ages in the transalpine states, politicians will have good reason to hope for the regeneration of Italy. Within the past three months, the geologists of ' Old Cornwall' have had proofs of activity in their favourite study by two smart earthquake shocks. The secoud was sufficiently severe to split a mass of masonry from top to bottom ar Newquay, tlnee miles north-west of Truro, and to shake hits of plaster from ceilings at St. Michael's Mount and elsewhere. þÿ Mr. Lieber, the government geologist of South Carolina, in a report on that state, shows proofs of ancient depressions along the coast, of total changes in the course of rivers, of subsequent elevation and extension seaward, succeeded by a depression which is now going on, accompanied bv what b" describes as 'a southward transitu v u of i uttoral islands ' This insular mo cement is accounted for by the set of a current, which wi-tes t >e nothorn end of

the islands, aud deposits the material at the southern end, and at such a rate that a part of the lluutitig Isles, where a sportsman still living shot his first buck, is now a hundred yards within the Atlantic. From Australia we hear of the opposite kind of pheuomeua, as published in the third volume of the Transactions of the Philosophical Institute of Victoria, which, in passiug, we may mention as highly interesting evidence of the pursuit of science in the eolouies. It appears from a series of observations, that in twelve months the bottom of Ilobson's Bay rose four inches ; that the beach at Williamstown, which, five years ago, was covered by the tide, is now covered with a green vegetation, and is the site of tents and houses. A foot below the present coast-road, a thick bed of sea-shells is found, at an elevation of eight feet above the present level of the hay. Whichever way the coast is followed, similar signs are met with. Flinders' soundings are no longer trustworthy, for where he found ten fathoms water, there are now but seven. The railway between Adelaide city and port rose four inches iu the year after it was opened ; aud considering these changes, the government of South Australia have ordered a new survey #(' the whole coast of that colony. The conclusion drawn from the several data is, that for some time a rise of four inches per annum has been going on ; if, therefore, the banks of the river at Melbourne have risen six feet within the past twenty years, it explains why the

wharfs are no longer, as formerly, liable to floods from the Yarra Yarra. Geologists have long boeu awtn'o that Australia is iu an unfinished condition, geologically speaking, as compared with other countries; and it may be that these changes are a part of the treatment which that great country has yet to undergo. ( I'm in Wednesday's Liberal. ) Bridgetown lias again bceu the scene of one of those dreadful conflagrations for which it is but too noted; and although on each occasion of the recurrence of these calamities the loss of property is immense, we are never prepared to grapple with the evil when it does overtake ns. ing Experience teaches waut induced through ns no wisdom. The suffer- of due precaution today makes us no more careful to provide a safeguard for to morrow. We talk a good deal of our uupreparedness, dwell very earnestly on jail the various points ol defieiency, and oensure the authorities without stint ; and there our efforts end. We do nothing beyond this either to secure ourselves or to stimulate the authorities to provide for us proper security such as is within reach of our means. The desolating fire of February 1845, caused a loss of many thousand pounds value in property, ruined numerous families, and completely destroyed a large portion of the lower part of the Town which has never been rebuilt. We have had warnings not a few since to provide against a similar calamity overtaking us in the upper and better portion of the Town ; and here we are utterly unprepared to meet it when it does actually come. A large and valuable portion of the upper part of the Town on this side the Careuage, and the Pier-head and lower part of Bay-street on the other side, present now heaps of smouldering

S- TV M 0 H V t » ruins. Property estimated at over £200,000 has been destroyed, and þÿGod providence s alone, aided by nothing that we ourselves did or could do in our utter unprepareduess, prevented that loss from being more than doubled. Tbe fire was discovered a little after 2 þÿo clock yesterday morning in the eountinghouse attached to the lumber-yard of Messrs. John and George H. Alleyno, Palmetto-street.
