THE PAPAL STATES. (From the Times Correspondent.) Rome, Jan. 25. I have some particulars to add to my yesterþÿday l s etter with respect to the popular demonstration of last Sunday evening; and these particulars are of a character to give the demonstration a far more important meaning than I was at first disposed to attach to it. In the first place, there is no doubt but the demonstration was altogether unprepared aud unexpected. It is usual for the French garrison to entertain the Roman people on Sunday and Thursday evenings with the music of their military bands, fanfares, &e.( at the time of the retreat, or evening roll-call. A great concourse of people had assembled at the Piazza Colonna on the evening in questiou, owing to the fine weather, and the return homewards of the many promenaders from the Pincio. It so happeued that a tall fair-haired man, apparently iu liquor, stood up in the midst of the crowd with a loud shout of þÿ Viva Bio Nono þÿ/ He was remonstrated with by some French gendarmes, as all cries, however loyal, are here strictly forbidden. He insisted upon his right to cheer his own liege Sovereign, whereupon he was hustled by the French gendarmes, and pushed back among the crowd, who visited his loyal enthusiasm with sundry kicks and blows, soundly and summarily administered, shouting all the while those hurrahs for þÿ tbb Emperor þÿ the French þÿ! þÿ þÿ! Italy þÿ the King! þÿ &c., to which 1 have alluded in my last. The French soldiery showed the greatest forbearance and good humour

towards the population, and allowed crowds to accompany them to their barracks, near the Cbiesa Nuova, though they so densely encompassed them that they that could I have been assured more than 5,000 per- scarcely move on. sons had gathered by the time the huge mass had reached the barracks. Here a French gendarme stood forth at the þÿbarracks door, waved his band, and, in broken Italian, intimated to the crowd that enough had been done for that evening, and that they might now, and should, all disperse and go quietly homo. The crowd complied with the most amiable docility, tbe assemblage broke up in the greatest order, and in a few minutes Rome regained its wonted tranquillity. The French Prefet of the Police, M. Mangin, has his residence in Piazza ColoDna, over the apartments of the French Club, and General Goyon lives in the Palazzo Ruspoli, in the Corso, before which the shouting multitude passed. Monsignor Mattouoci, the Minister of the Pontifical Police, who had not heard one word of tbe row in the evening, received his first information from the French authorities on the morrow. General Goyon, in his excessive zeal lor the cause of the Papacy, came, with Monsiguor Matteucci, to the resolution of temptiug (lie people to a renewal of the demonstration, aud laid with the Roman police the programme of tho evening performance. Contrary to the custom, which limits the playing of the band and fanfare to the evenings of Sunday and Thursday, orders were given to the musicians
to repair to tho Piazza Colonna on that very

evening (Monday). Drummers and trumpeters, with all their klingendes spiel, came on, preceded by a company of Chasseurs, followed by a company of Fusileers, the mighty martial retinuo closing with a troop of 30 to 40 mounted Papal carabineers, or gendarmes. The wretched sloppy weather, and the actual rain, to a great exteut marred the sport the authorities expected to enjoy. Vast crowds assembled, nevertheless, partly attracted l»y the report of the demonstration of the previous evening, partly by the novelty of the band playing on such a dismal night. The people, however, behaved in the most exemplary manner, listened to the music, and contented themselves with following the band on its departure. They followed the line of the Corso as far as the street which leads to the barracks, passed the Borghesc Palace, under the windows of which a few hisses were heard, and arrived at a spot called Monte Brionzo, where a few cries of þÿ Vive þÿNapoleon!' were heard. The Papal gendarmes who closed the march stood still immediately, and, turning their horses, galloped back upon the people, who forthwith dispersed, a great many taking refuge in a large doorway haid by. The gendarmes pursued the multitude up to this place of shelter, where they were mot by five Freuch Chasseurs, who, covering the retreat of the people, met their pursuers with a gallant and resolute þÿ Vive þÿI Empereur þÿ! The Papal gendarmes pulled up at the sight, and again turning rein, walked away after the band, þÿ with their tails between

their þÿlegs, followed, as a matter of course, by the triumphant multitude, who now shouted lustily and exultiugly, thronging on the hoofs of their crest-fallen antagonists. This was on the Monday evening. Last night the Piazza Colouna was crowded with French soldiers, chiefly Chasseurs, not on duty, talking and gesticulating together in animated groups. As on the previous evening all the streets leading, to the Piazza Colonna were beset with Papal gendarmes, and perambulated by patrols, generally consisting of a Papal gendarme followed by three French soldiers. Companies of French iufantrv of the line, with their officers at their head, were seen marching to and fro; the people, however, had not mustered in very formidable numbers, and nothing occurred to give either party an opportunity for a display of their feelings. I am told, nevertheless, that public expectation is on the tiptoe as to what may happen on Thursday next, the evening on which the Roman people look forward to their regular entertainment of the evening band, and cannot fail to assemble in large masses in the Colonna-square. From all these facts, on the correctness of which reliance may be put, you may infer þÿ peror Napoleon to give the Pope and his Gofirst, that the Roman people have been dragged to these demonstrations quite against their will. The popular leaders, known here as þÿ the Comþÿmittee,- have shown the greatest distress at tile disturbance, and have used their best exertion to prevent its recurrence. There is cer-

tainly great excitement and exasperation among the Romans of all classes, provoked by those very unmeaning and very superfluous addresses by the Roman nobility, by the College Physicians, of and several other collegiate bodies, and by the parish priests venturing to speak in the name of their parishioners, representing the Papal subjects as marvellously delighted with his þÿlloliness s government. The Romans are bent upon giving these selfconstituted interpreters of the popular mind the lie direct. They take every opportunity iu the theatres, whether the performance be tragical or comical, to find iu the most harmless sentence or word the actors may utter allusions to present circumstances. Already the Cleopatra at the Teatro Capronica, the Caravanna, at the Teatro Valle, and Chi dura vince, at the Teatro Argentina, have been either curtained or wholly suppressed, þÿ this latter, an opera, thojwords, simply because þÿ Povero in a certain duet there occurred Giovanni !" þÿ Povero Sennoro and the people took up the strain with infinite laughter, applying the first name to Giovanni Mastai-Ferretti (the Pope), and the second to the King of Naples, both of whom they pitied utterly as undone. It seems hardly worth while to report such silly incidents were it not that out of mere insipid farces serious evils arise to some of the parties concerned in them. þÿ1 ulcinella, or Punch, was arrested at the Argentina Theatre for some allusions to majali neri (black swine,), which, he said, must be killed, and killed safely

& n. o i ; & wa s. upon ( accorati ), lest they become dangerous; þÿ the whole audience rose, crying, where- Accorali, accorati, i neri," (Kill them, kill them all, the Blacks þÿ i. e., the priests,). Other more serious arrests were effected last night, probably in consequence of the harmless demonstration oflast Sunday; among others Luigi Gulminelli and Fedeli, with three of bis sons, all belonging to the respectable classes, with other more obscure individuals Sant.-Angeli, whose imprisonment was made the theme of so at much talk a few weeks ago, and was released the solicitation of the French Government, was summoned before the police yesterday to give a minute account of the manner in which he had employed every day' and hour of the time subsequent to bis deliverance. Notwithstanding this unsettled state of the public mind, it seems very clear that the Romans would not have ventured upon any steps which might be construed into a breach of the law without the provocation, on Sunday, of the tall, fair-haired man, who was in all probability, an agent of the police. It seems also very clear that the French troops, or part of them at least, are rather unwilling instruments in the hands of the Papal Government, and that their commander, General Goyon, whose zeal for the Holy See is so notorious that the Romans sent him as a present a þÿJesuit sbroad-brimmed hat and soutane, and whom his soldo rs liick-n nmeje Maine, will have some difficulty in using them at a pinch against the people, with whom they have

already shown some symptoms of incipient fraternization. The sending of the baud on Monday evening, contrary to all custom, was explained by the authorities as a mere display of force, a bravado to show the Multitude that the Government would not suffer a deliberate repetition of an outrage of which only surprise secured the impunity. It had all the appearance of a wanton provocation, m veitheless, and suspicious are rife among the Romans that the whole object of the Papal Government and of the superior French officers was to bring about a collision between the multitude and the half-sympathizing French soldiers, which might put an end for ever to any chance of a good understanding between them. We have seen that the result was very nearly the contrary, as a conflict was on the point of arising between the French Chasseurs and the Papal Carabineers. The situation, however, is extremely ominous in Rome and fraught with imminent danger, and the Romans are perhaps right iu their assertion that General Goyon has written to his Government, either to recall him or to supply him with more reliable troops. I should not wonder if it entered into the views of the Em-

vernment some salutary evidence of their utter helplessness, so as to have them mote manageable and amenable to his enlarged and far-sighted policy ; neither should I be surprised it the Pope, the moment lie became aware of any wavering in the allegiance of the French troops, bethought himself of seeking at Benevento, Gaeta, or the Balearic Isles, a safer and less gloomy and uncomfortable refuge than he may hope to find in those catacombs to which he always talks of resorting, to add one more to the many martyrs whose bones are mouldering aud bleaching in their impervious recesses.

FRANCE. A General commanding one of the divisions of the army of this department is said to have received orders last week to prepare to move with his troops for Italy. The order was countermanded the following day. Military officers are to be attached to the French Embassies accredited to the Courts of England, Austria, Prussia, and Russia. Lieutenant-Colonel Colson, of the Staff-Corps, goes to St. Petersburg ; Chef þÿd Escadrou (Staff) þÿd Audelan to Vienna ; the Prince de Bauffremetit, Chef þÿd Escadron, 6th Hussars, to Berlin ; and Chef þÿd Escadron þÿd Audigue te Loudon. There is a rumour of the re-establishment of the camp at Chalons. I have received the following letter : þÿ þÿ A deputation of the most distinguished Protestants of Hungary has gone to Vienna to represent to the Emperor the danger he will incur if he persists in entorcing his hated patent on the Protestants. From, however, the scant intelligence and the notorious obstinacy of the Emperor, and from the stupidity of his counsellors, tho members of the deputation have not

the slightest hope that he will attend to their representations, and their only object in making them is to prove to Hungary and to Europe that they have done all that in them lies to preserve peace with the Viennese Government, aud that, in consequence, they will be in nowise responsible tor the events that may follow from its wicked and reckless policy. I informed you in my preceding letter that the Austrian Government, was resolved, iu spite of the universal and indignant remonstrances of all Protestant Hungary, to carry out the aforesaid patent. It has begun doing so in the county of Arva, which is peopled by Slovacks; and the reason why it selects that county in preference to any other is that for local circumstances it possesses some influence there, and that the Slovacks not being of the same race as the Hungarians have hitherto not been quite so hostile to the Hapsburg family. But even in Arva it has encountered an energetic resistance. Under the able direction of M. Kubinyi, president of the superintending commission of the district, the Protestants of the county have refused to take part in the election of elders, or to do any other act whatever towards the carrying out of the patent. I have received a letter from a Protestant cleigyman in the county, which says, þÿ We are surprised that the agents of the Ilapsburgs should presume to think that we are more disposed than our Protestant brethren in other pans of the kingdom to submit to the odious patent. We are determined, on the

coutrary, as they are, to oppose it by every means iu our power short of actual violence. We will do so with the calmness that becomes Christians, but at the same time with the resolution that becomes þÿmen. When such is the language and such the conduct of the Protestants who the Viennese Government flutters itself are the þÿ faithful among the faithless þÿfound, judge what the people of the rest of Hungary will say and do. In the great crisis into which the Protestant religion of Hungary is plunged, the eyes of all sincere defenders of the faith arc turned towards England. The Hungarians feel certain that she looks with interest on their sufferings, aud with sympathy for their efforts, and they are not without hope that her Parliament will, in imitation of her noble press, raise its voice in their behalf. On this last point 1 have reason to believe that they will not be mistaken. I know that more than oue member of each of the two Houses lias put himself into communication with the leaders of tho Protestants in this þÿcountry in , order to obtain a detailed statement of the grievances ot the Protestant churches and of the oppression of the Hungarian people, and 1 know that a political personage in England, who is familiar with the situation of þÿHungary , has written that if the English Government did its duty it would send some such message to the Viennese Cabinet as that which Cromwell sent to a Pope þÿ namely, that þÿ if lie dared to oppress the people of God, English cannon

stiould thunder at St. þÿAngelo. þÿ AUSTRIA. The Trieste Zcitung learns from Milan th«t the three Sardinian brigades which are to occupy Parma, Modena, aud the Romagna have been appointed. Fourteen hundred Piedmontese are already in Mirandola, þÿ and it is a positive fact that the French army in Lombardy is receiving reinforcements from þÿFrance. The French and Sardinian troops have recently changed some of their positions, so that the former are now nearer the frontier of Venetia. þÿ Powerful French detachments are now in Brescia and Desenzano, and some French cavalry has even been pushed forward to þÿGoito. In Milan a speedy invasion of Venetia is talked of, and the points of attack are to be the districts of Revere, Scrmide, and Gonzaga, on the right bank of the Po. On tho 19th iust. some armed men appeared in Borghetto, a small place opposite Valleggio, and insulted aud fired at, though without wounding, a picket of Kaiser Jagers. Very many persons have been arrested in Venice during the last few days. 20 Finance employes, who quitted Mantua without leave, have been summoned by the Provincial Finance Direction to return to their posts immediately. It is now certain that the Austrian Government does not intend to interfere in Central Italy. In a day or two you will doubtless hear from your correspondent at Naples that mischief is brewing there, The Neapolitan Government is greatly alarmed, and sees in every foreigner an agent of Murat.

The Theory of Earthquakes. þÿ Professor Rogers, of Glasgow University, in the course of a lecture delivered recently, in the "Merchants' Hall, on "Volcanic Action, with especial reference to the Theory of Eearthquakes," treated of the different species of volcanic eruptions, such as hot steam, lava, stones, earth, and then proceeded to the special subject of earthquakes. These, he said, were composed of a pulsating motion, which was of colossal magnitude, attd connected with which was a tremulous jarring þÿ a shudder of the earth þÿ accompanied by a crackling of the rocky matter. An earthquake took its time to a minute, and observers could consequently calculate its velocity. It was composed of a group of advancing waves, and its average period of oscillation was two or three minutes. In the year 1812 the town of Caraccas, in America, was destroyed, and the valley of the Mississippi was also affected. The backwoodsmen in the Western States at that period, who had their senses all awake, discovered that this earthquake came from the direction of the Mississippi, and that when the earth yawned, the fissures ran north and south. To save themselves being engulphed, they cut down trees, which they caused to fall east and west, and as soon as they felt the tremulous movement, they left their cabins and bestrode the trees. The result of the investigations which he had made into several earthquakes that had occurred in the West Indies and in America, was, that the undulating waves

in the interior of the earth moved forward at a speed of from 27 to 34 miles per minute, leaving a crust upon the rocks with which they came in contact. In some parts of the world the earthquakes had completely changed the surface ol the earth ; the swamps of Missouri having, for instance, been transformed into a rich soil, dotted with shallow lakes. A port at the mouth of the Indus had been sunk beneath the surface of the water ; and the strata of the Alleghany Mountains also bore marks of the influence of these underground currents. Electro-Magnetism applied to Weaving. þÿ An improvement in weaving-machinery, the importance of which can scarcely be overrated, has been introduced by a M. Bonelli, who had made use of a simple electro-magnetic apparatus, in place of the elaborate system of cards invented by Jacquard. The peculiarity of the Jacquard loom consists in the use of perforated pieces of card-board, through the holes in which sotne of the wires, or small rods, one ol which is attached to each thread in the warp, are allowed to slip, and thus raise these threads, while the others are opposed to solid portions of the card. In the new invention the design traced in black varnish on the tinfoil paper is placed in the band as an endless band over a roller. A row of thin brass plates, terminating in points, touches with these points the patterns in an horizontal line right across it. These touching plates correspond in number with the threads of the warp ; the pole of a

tinfoil of the pattern. magnetic battery is in The contact with the electric current passes through the tinfoil, and enters every brass-plate in contact with it, which stands on the bare surface of the tin. The black varnish of the pattern is a non-conductor, and prevents the electricity from passing into any of the brass, plates touching the varnished portion of the tinfoil. Now, t e electric current passing through any one of these brass plates is made to magnetise a little iron rod. The magnetised rod attracts another rod, and, by the aid of mechanism, the corresponding thread of the warp is elevated.

The Nnrd of Friday publishes the text of the important dispatch, addressed on the 30th uit. to the French Ambassador at Londou, by M Thouvenel, Minister of Foreign Affairs, in reply to the propositions of the British Government, already made kuown in the House of Commons. To the proposition of non-intervention the French Government giv. s its implicit adherence The proposition that the French troops quit the Roman States and Lombardy is acceded to by the Imperial Government, on conditions such as that Rome is not evacuated until the Holy See is secured from danger ; nor the Lontbaid provinces "until the agreement, either tacit or avowed, of the Great Powers, shall have guaranteed the new organisation of Italy." The third point, as to Venetia, does not excite any objections ; hut at the same time it must be left open to consider any Concessions which Austria may at a future time offer with regard to Venetia. In treating of the fourth proposition þÿ viz., that the King of Sardinia be invited: by the Governments of France and Great Britain, acting in concert, to send no troops into Central Italy until the different States and Provinces have, by a vote of their Assemblies after a new election, solemnly declared tie ir wisln s, aud if these Assemblies pronounce in favour ol annexation, France and Gieat Britain shall not any longer oppose the entry of the Sardinian troops. M. de Thouvenel enlarges upon tin fruitless endeavours which France lias made for

several months to carry out the provisions of the Ti Caty of Zurich ; 'hut," continues tie Mi uister, "whatever may be our opinion upon the value of the combination in which the British Government takes the initiative, we regard ourselves morall' obliged to previously opel) it' go tin t ions Upon it with the Austrian Court. M must maintain the loyalty of the Emperor and the sincerity of his policy above all suspicion, and we could not to-day, in the presence of the stipulations of Villairanea and Zurich, pledge ourselves in a formal manner, ll tin incflieacy of our counsels and of our proceedings has shown us the impossibility of re-establishing the authority of deposed Princes, we arc not tin less bound to prevent tiny false interpretation, and to remove all doubts in first r deeming the word of France in loyal explanations with the Court of Austria. Moreover, we should not forget that we but lately invited Russia ami Prussia to join in a Congress, the meeting of which seemed to assure at once an understanding between the Powers, and to t repare the solution of the questions which would have been submitted to its deliberations. It has not been our fault that Europe so assembled was not called to consecrate a definite arrangement, and we should fear to expose ourscdves to wound national susceptibilities, if, finding ourselves brought now by the fore of events to another point of view, wo were to abstain from pointing out to the Cabinets of St. Petersburg and Berlin i the new situation created for us by imperious
circumstances, and if we were to neglect to 1 convince them of tb necessity of seeking more

practical means of regulating the questions, which cannot, without danger, be left very much longer in suspense. I have then replied to Lord Cowley as to the fourth proposition, that the Government of the Emperor, before pronouncing upon it, believes its it indispensable explain and to justily situation with the to Court of Austria on the one hand, and with those of Prussia and Prussia on the other. The English Ambassador appeared to me to appreciate the motives which impose this lrne of conduct upon the Imperial Government, and I have confidence that the English Government will recognize its justice and force. The reception which we have given to its first three piopnsitions will prove, if it were necessary, the sentiments in which we have received its overtures, aud it cannot have any doubt as to our sincere desire to combine the solutions which the situation of Central Italy calls for and permits." The pretext for this movement is the. apprehension of an invasion of the Marches by the King of Naples, hut the real cause i.s to be louud in the difficulties which have arisen between Franco and Piedmont relative to t lie annexation of Nice and Savoy to the former, and the annexation of Central Italy to the latter."

withstanding ail this, the continue the policy ot' Spain will general opinion to be one of is that observation so long as Europe shall remain undisturbed by grave events."

From the bmnHon Times, Febr. 17. The sever ii answers of Lord John Russell last night in the House of Commons explain perfectly the present position of affairs with respect to the annexation of Savoy. The Foreign Secretary sufficiently indicated the grave state of lite question, and the tone of liis replies was an earnest that no effort will he spared hy the British Cabinet to prevent so wanton a wrong as t lie dismemberment of the Sardinian Monarchy. Lord John Russell stated that communications had passed between the British and Sardinian Governments, that the former had inquired whether there was an engagement or intention to cede Savoy to France, and that the answer had been generally that there was no engagement on the subject, and that Sardinia had no intention to cede Savoy.

s T-. c B 0 I X ft V/ I) S « So far the information given to the House was perfectly satisfactory. It seemed clear that, whatever discussions may It >ve taken place on this subject before and since the war, King Victor Emmanuel bad never consented to relinquish. bis most ancient province, and that he will now resist both temptations and menaces, from whatever quarter they may come. The continuation of Lord John Russell's remarks was, however, calculated to excite anxiety, and it called up Mr. Seymour Fitzgerald. Lord John Russell, in answer to a question concerning the neutrality of Switzerland, spoke of what the Government intended to do "in case of annexation," and observed that be had been afraid Switzerland, induced by the offer of certain districts, would favour annexation, but was happy to assure the House that such fears had proved groundless. As from these remarks it was evident that annexation was really imminent, Mr. Seymour Fitzgerald put a further question, and then the whole truth came out. In fact, Sardinia lias not agreed to cede Savoy, and does riot wish or intend to do so, but the French Emperor lias demanded Savoy as the price ot his consent to the annexation of Hie Italian Duchies and the Homagna to the dominions of Victor Emmanuel. " It has," said Lord John Russell, "to "my " the Government knowledge been communicated to ot Turin that if the "kingdom " to any considerable extent aggrandized of Sardinia were by the an- " nexatiou ot' Central Italy, France "would think that her frontier was not

"secure without the annexation til at "least some part of Savoy." Such, then, is the latest development of the Italian question. The Emperor of the French, in whose strange character the two opposing qualities of vigour and vacillation seem to meet, is now, at the eleventh hour, endeavouring to throw difficulties in the way of that Italian union to which lie had apparently given his consent. It is plain that the demand tor a part of Savoy is as much intended to dissuade the King from extending his dominions southward as to induce hint to give France the French slopes of the Alps. The demand is, in tact, a return to the policy upon which the Emperor entered in May last, when 1'rinee Napoleon was sent to Tuscany to head the revolution. Then it was | scarcely concealed, though it lias been vehemently denied since, that the plan was to establish a kingdom in Central Italy under the sceptre of the Prince whose marriage had united the Houses of France and Sardinia. Events marched, however, too quickly for the fortunes of the Prince. Roth war arid revolution left him far behind. Austria was driven from Lombardy in a few weeks, and before the French division, with the new Tuscan levies, could be brought into the field. There was no opportunity for them to show their valour against the Austrians, for the Austrinns were swept away before Prince Napoleon bad time to reach the Mincio. The Emperor seems then to have abandoned bis earlier scheme, and to have made peace with as little thought for his cousin as for

his ally. Thus the scheme for an independent kingdom of Etruria would have perished had the people been as passive and as submissive to the despotism of potentates as 60 years ago. But the Tuscans and their brethren had tasted independence, and were not inclined to give it up even to please the liberator of Lombardy. They determined on an-

nexation to Sardinia, and have been since sis hostile to the formation of a separate kingdom as to the restoration of their former Sovereign. The world had thought within the last few months that the French Emperor had made up bis mind to accept the annexation to Sardinia, and that the renewed alliance with England was a pledge of this wise policy. But it is one of the shortcomings of si despotic Government that so much is left to a single mind, which the habit of irresponsibility is apt to make capricious. The French Emperor lias seemingly sacrificed everything to the policy which England has had the credit of initiating. He has declared to the Viennese Court that be will not restore the Italian Sovereigns, nor allow Austrian troops to enter the rebellious territory. He has thus exposed himself to the charge of violating the Treaty of Zurich, and the press of Austria and Southern Germany lias been pouring forth invectives against him for the last three months as a traitor. Then he has broken utterly and irrevocably with t lie Pope. He lias sanctioned a pamphlet containing political doctrines which no Protestant statesman has ventured to propound; lie lias enforced the submission of the French priesthood with a high hand, forbidding the publication of episcopal manifestoes and suppressing the most notorious organ of th'e clergy. English politicians may lie excused for believing that all this portended the acceptance of Italian nationality, for they cannot conceive

how a ruler should take so much trouble and expose himself to so much obloquy without having finally made up his mind. Now, however, after having declared that the people of Central Italy shall not be interfered with, and having thus acquiesced iu the annexation of their country to Sardinia, Napoleon comes forward and tells Victor Emmanuel at what a price he must purchase the permission to accept the sovereignty which is tendered to him. So preposterous a pretence as that put tortli hy the French Government for the annexation of Savoy has probably never come under the notice of Europe. France, with a standing army of 600,000 men, with a powerful fleet, with a system of railways constructed expressly with a view to the carriage of troops, with a compact territory, with a centralized administration, and with every State in Europe anxious for its internal tranquility, affects to view with alarm the formation of a too extensive kingdom in Italy. " If Sardi- " nia be aggrandized to any considerable " extent France would think that Iter " frontier was not secure without the " annexation of some part of Savoy." We really wonder that any Government should venture at the present day to put forward such a pretext. Statesmen may often say what they do not believe, hut it argues a cynical contempt for opinion to utter that which they cannot expect to be believed by others. We can hardly think that the Emperor Napoleon will persist in a scheme so much at variance with the character for justice and mode-

During last, year, the number of Coolies and liberated Africans in trod need was 30,910. Of this number 9,496, or about a third, eatno to the West Indies, the rest went to Mauritius Of the forme , (the West Indian Immigrants), 7,719 were Coolies, and 1 þÿ 77 Africans. Besides these, there were 699 from China, 1,048 from Madeira, 4 from St. Helena, and 20 from Havana. It may be added, that by far the greater number of these Immigrants went to Demerara and Trinidad ; iu consequence of which addition to the Labouring Population, the crops ol these two Colonies have increased. Late papers from Demerara give us the following list of Immigrants, amounting to 1,400, between the 9th and 17th April : þÿ þÿ April 9th þÿ Ship Bed Biding Hood, 71 days form Chinn, with 311 Chinese. 1 1th þÿ Barque St. Cnix, 94 days from Calcutta, with 172 Coolies. 13th þÿ Barqe Priam 69 days from Madras, , with 257 Coolies.

« T. g R i G X ft VI) 14th þÿ Ship Calliopo , 91 days from Calcutta, with 325 Coolies and 30 captured Africans. 17th þÿ Ship Colgrain, 86 days from Madras, with 291 þÿCoolies. þÿ The Ship Bed Biding Hoad from China came in yesteiday with 311 immigrants. She took in 314 at Hong-Kong, but one woman died in child-birth, one man committed suicide by jumping overboard, and another fell overboard aud was drowned, so that no death occurred on the passage from disease of any kind. The Whirlwind, which was the first, vessel of the season, arrived on the 12th March with 377 Chinese, no deaths on the passage ; then came the Bora ou the 3rd instant with 385, having lost 4 on the wav, one by suicide aud two others from natural causes ; and on the Sth instant the Bed Riding Hood, with 311, and loss of three as above mentioned. Suicides could not he prevented, and a death in child-birth is unfortunately a matter of too common occurrence to call for particular notice. Shutting out this last case, the suicides and the accident of a man falling overboard, we have three vessels arriving, within a short period of each other, with 1,073 immigrants, only three having died on board from ordinary causes. It is hut a fair conclusion, according to the calculation as to duration of life, that had the 1,076 immigrants remained ashore instead of taking the long voyage to this colony, at least an equal number of them would have died during the same period of þÿtime. There is a great outcry raised by the Antislavery Party in Englund against this Immigra-

tion, on the score of the mortality and ill-treatment of the Immigiants on the passage from the East to the West. But the above statement will compare favorably even with the Irish and Gentian Immigrants across the Atlantic into the United States iu this respect, and affotds a striking contrast to the burrowing details attending the transit of about 1000 British Sohlieis Horn Calcutta to Liverpool, in the Great Tasmania , as copied from the English papers into the last West Indian. A Strange Story. þÿ A sad event, unfortunately not unique in the annals of science, has just occurred here. Some time ago a lady, of supetior talent as governess in private families, had confided to her care a little Russian hoy, born deaf and dumb. The child was of gentle temper and endearing manners, and the poor governess bent, the whole of her intelligence to the possibility of instructing him to keep pace with her other pupils. Soon, at sight of his quick comprehension of the various methods she invented for his instruction, she began to grow more ambitious still, and to be devoured with the desire to endow him with the faculty which Nature herself had denied For this purpose it appears that Mademoiselle Cleret spent whole nights in study, and lavished her slender means in experiments. At length the light broke in upon her. She remained perfectly convinced that in sulphuric ether must reside the talisman powerful enough to restore the deaf to a sense of hearing. She began by pouring into the ear a few drops only at a time, gradually increasing the quantity until it reached 10 drops, þÿl he cure was complete. The child heard and understood in a short time. The articulation was still imperfect for a little while longer, but that, it seems, lias since yielded to surgical treatment. The fame of the cure spread far and near. The remedy was tried upon numberless individuals in all stages of deafness, and in every case succeeded. A commission was named to pronounce upon the discovery made by Mademoiselle Cleret.

The decision was made wholly in its favour, the Montyon prize was awarded to the fortunate lady, and various testimonials of favour < re conveyed to her both from public bodies and private individuals. But the end of this sacrifice and devotion to the cause of humanity is sad to toll. Poor Mademoiselle Cleret, unable to resist the change from a position of dependence and privation to one of fame and comparative opulence, has sunk beneath the weight of t ho unexpected honours thus conferred upon her. Her mind, worn out with study and anxiety, worn nut with labour and with watching, has given way, and she has just been conveyed a hopeless maniac to a m :ison de sanle at Mont martre. þÿ Letter from Paris.

Life on the Moon. Until quite recently, the surface of the moon has been supposed to be a vast lifeless desert,. Astronomers have abused the moon in every possible way. They have said there was no heat in moonshine. They have denied the moon an atmosphere, and consequently water and organic life. They have made us believe that a residence in the moon would be exceedingly undesirable. The old faith in the Goddess of the Night was quite overturned in scientific circles, and the fascinations of moonlight were departing day by day. But this is all changed. Knox and Melloni have shown, by very exact observation, that there is heat in the þÿmoon s rays. Zantsdeschi has discovered that this heat produces a sensible effect upon the mimosa. An English philosopher has found that the earth is colder during the first quarter of the moon than it is in the second. Upon the growth of plants the moon exercises a remarkable influence. The chemical action of life is necessary to their principal work, the absorption of carbon from the carbonic acid gas of the atmosphere. This work all plants carry on during the day, and in the night they sleep þÿ except when the moon shines. She wakes them and sets them at work. So the farmers who plant only just before the full moon are right, and the scoffers who call them superstitious are themselves the foolish ones For, if sown before or near new moon, the young plants get above ground just at the full, when the tender things need sleep. But if sown just before

the full, they come up about new moon, j pass their babyhood under the soothing influences of dark nights, and when the full moon comes are sturdy urchins, able to work night and day. The moon-wor- j shipers are right, also, in regard to the influence of the moon upon the weather. Herschel, Arago and Whewell recognized that the moon had some slight power in dispersing clouds. At the last meeting of the British As ociation, it was shown that the weather through a long series of years depended a littleþÿ a very little þÿ upon the phases of the moon, and now Quetelet, the -Director of the Brussels Observatory, has shown that between the first and last quarters of the moon more and not less rain falls than during the remainder of the time. However, fine weather and greater rain fall may go together. Finally, Webb, after a careful comparison of the present appearance of the moon with the very precise maps made by Madler some twenty years ago, has shown that there have been considerable changes. Some of the small craters, in particular, have a notably different form from what they had when Miidler observed of them. These changes show the existence water and an atmosphere. Father Secchi, Director of the Roman Observatory, after much observation, has come to the conclusion that the peaks of the highest mountains on the moon are covered with snow. And to make us still more at home on the moon, De la Rive, the owner of the observatory at Crawford, near London, gives it as his opinion, that what were at first

marked down as seas, and afterwards supposed to be barren plains, are in fact extensive forests. In support of this, comes up a great astronomic authority, Schwabe, the discoverer of the periodic times of the þÿsun sspots. Besides these great smooth plains, which were called seas, there are a number of furrows or wrinkles, nearly a hundred, the nature of which waR entirely unknown. 1 þÿfjfi CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 25th MAY, 1S60. In a few days Ilis Excelleney Governor Schlegel will resign the government of these Colonies into other hands. Ilis þÿExcellency s administration has been a quiet and orderly one. If we cannot point to any very important measures carried out by him, the fault can unquestionably only be ascribed to the very limited powers with which he has been entrusted. Circumscribed in his sphere of usefulness by a ministry, thousands of miles distant, whose chief object, in reference to the colonies, has been to prepare popular Budgets, and to force all other interests to accord with the financial one, we could naturally not expect much from his administration.

S T >. C B 0 I X AVI , His Excellency, we are sure, will leave us with more enlarged views ol the inhabitants of these Colonies, than those with which he came among us. Unfortunately, it is to be feared that the mass of the population of Denmark share much of the feelings and sentiments of men of the Lehman stamp. The egregious blunders of this individual in the Landsthing, during the Session of 1856, will be remembered as having called forth a great deal of contempt from among the intelligent portion of this ence ot men who have been among us, community. It is only through the influ- in positions where information of our condition, hopes and interests can be obtained, that we may hope to have removed the mists which obscure the view taken of us in the mother-country. We therefore hope, that, iu whatever sphere of life His Excellency on his return home may enter, we may count on his friendly ollices. The interests of these Colonies have long been sacrificed for the benefit ot the mother-country. This state of things, we fear, cannot lastmuch longer without entailing inevitable ruin on them. In that Mr. þÿLehman opinions, s we think spite of Ilis þÿExcellency e s xperience will have proved to him that no other subjects of Denmark are more loyal than those in her West- Iudia colonies. Notwithstanding that the policy of .the mother-country has not been such as to draw closer the ties between her and us, yet it is in the hope that justice will one day be done to us, that we patiently await to that legal manner have day, and strive in a our wants made

known. We are hold enough to express the hope that our future government will partake more of a popular character. If the local government would but join its advice to our endeavours we have no fear of obtaining more liberal institutions. With a salubrious climate and a population of a peaceful disposition, if but steps are taken in the right direction, these Colonies may yet hope to re-enter on mutual which would be of a state ot prosperity benefit to them and to Denmark.

The population of the Islands consists almost entirely of natives, whose disposition l>y nature is mild and not inclined to premeditated violence ; they have for generations been treated with forbearance and justice, and influenced by a numerous and enlightened clergy, and baveforyears bad the advantage of respectable school-establishment. This population is and þÿought þÿespecially in the larger island of Sr Croix þÿ to be referred to seek their snpp it principally by agriculture, and is in consequence pretty evenly distributed over the whole island ; they can at all times obtain remunerative occupation and work, and are, in a material point of view, advantageously situated. With the preceding considerations in view, the Council must recommend a considerable reduction of the present military force and i principally of the expenditure for this branch ; being fully convinced, that this burthen is heavier than can be borne by the colours in their present circumstances, without destroying essential conditions of any future improvement. During the debates, an opinion has been expressed, that the military force, might, with perfect safety, be reduced to 200 soldiers and a corresponding number of officers, about equally divided between St. Croix and St. .Thomas, but < as there exist feelings on this subject, which deserve proper consideration, the Colonial Council cannot propose so great a reduction, but shall recommend that steps be taken without delay, for a reorganisation as would iusure

a decrease in the military expenditure of at least $25,000 pr. annum. Under the discussion on this subject, it has been advanced that such a saving might be secured, by limiting the pres lit force of 550 men, þÿ officers and non-commissioned officers included, þÿ to a force of 390, one company being stationed in St. Thomas, and the two coinpaniesinSt. Croix beingreduced to 200 men, andby doing away with the separate garrison in Fre- 1 very dcriksted, the service there being performed by a detachment, commanded by one officer, in which case a separate garrison-physician and military-hospital would not be required there. It is not thought neivsso y to k op the forts in St. Croix and their armament towards the sea in a state calculated for defence against foreign attack, for which purpose they are entirety unfit. With regard to an occasionally occurring want of officers for service, should this number be reduecd, it is supposed that such a difficulty is at present of less consequence, considering the efficiency of the class of non-commissioned officers at present. It must, however, always be left to t tie Governor, at any time, according to circumstances, to increase or diminish the | should always have a healthy and pleasant reforces at the different stations. Being convinced that such a giving ought and cau be obtained, the Council lias with 9 votes to 3 agreed to propose : þÿ that the item sub B. e. 2, for military expenses $115,000 be reduced witli þÿ$25,000. The Government has recommended several

additional items of expenditure, hitherto Dot allowed, viz: an increase of $200 pr. annum to the oldest first-lieutenant attached to the troops, until he be advanced to captain, furthermore a sum of $192, as the expense inenred for quarters for the garrison-physician in Frederiksted, as ! frequently well as $500 to a band-master. The Council finds no objections to these proposals, provided, that the expenditure incurred thereby can he covered by the amouut of $90,000 proposed for military expenses. The same is applicable with regard to a petition for an increase of pay for officers after a certain time of service, and it has with 8 votes to 4 been agreed upon to recommend an increase, proposed by a member, for such officers as are permanently attached to the force, after 20 years service in the colonies, viz : an increase every 4 years of $200 for commanders of the forts, and the depot, and $100 for subaltern officers. Ad B. c 3. Buildings and other uncertain expenses. The proposed increase of this item, formerly $20,000, by additional $5000, arises, as appears from the explanations communicated.

St B HO) (1 AVIS. from the intended repairs of the governmenthouse at Christiansted, besides the cost of materials, purchased during the last financial year with an outlay of $5,648 .90 cents; there is calculated for those repaiis an amount of about $9 to 10,000, part of which it is supposed will he expended in the financial year 1860-61. As the Council, in connection with the proposal to the item sub B. e. 5, concerning the purchase of Bulowsininde, has proposed a consider- i able limitation of the intended lepairs of the governmenthouse at Christiansted, we would hereby recommend : that the item of expenditure sub B. e. 3, þÿ buildings and other uncertain þÿexpenses lie reduced by $5000. AdB.c. 4 As it is explained in the motives, that, this amount has been entered in the Colonial- budget only as a, temporary measure, not tending to the abolition of the present rules concerning such exjienses ; the Council does not think that there is cause to offer any7 further remarks to this item. Ad B. e. 5. $10,000 for the purchase of Bulowsminde. According to the explanations communicated, the þÿGovernment proposal .- is to ibis effect: a, that the place with all its appurtenances and 63 acres of land, besides the present furniture (the latter valued at $2198) be purchased by the Statctieasury as a country-residence for the Governor. 4, that the future nccessaiy expenses for the conservation of the property and the buildings, be defiayed by the Statetrea-ury, Gut that the tepair and renewals of the furniture do not

concern the treasury, c, that as a consideration of the accommodation thus secured for ihe Givernoi, he retained $600 p. a., of his salary. The pi ice of $10,000 demanded for it is low, compared to what the buildings have co.-t, and must even under pre.-ent circumstances be considered as cheap. The buildings are built of the very best materials, and þÿ as observed in the Governþÿment s explanations þÿ they ate on the whole in good order, and will only require some not considerable repairs, the expenses of which as well as the taxes, ought to be fully covered by the average amount of $000, as mentioned above. From what we have stated above, the question is not of any new anutiil expense, but solely the outlay of the $10,000 demanded once for all. As to the qiii sti.in, if there is sufficient cause to accept the opportunity offered to purchase this propci ty for the n-e intended and at the price demanded, we consider, that the question ought lo he answered affirmatively, even making every allowance lor the present depressed State of i he island. It is only proper and consistent with the views ef the population, that the Governor

sidence proper for his official position and convenient for himself and his family These requirements we think would he fully satisfied by the purchase of Bulowsminde, whereas these have lutheito not been considered as satisfied by the residence in the government- | house, on account of its low situation, poor arrangements and want of proper connection of I the buildings. These defects can not either be remedi d by a re-building or alterations of government buuse Even if it was or could he made better and mme comfortable, it would he desirable and not seldom necessary, that i lie Governor and his family have an opp -rt unity to live in the country. From what is staled above we would recommend the Government's proposal, however on this express condition, that a considerable reduction be made in the amount of expenses for I the extensions and repairs of the present governmenthouse, which as now planned would cost more than $15,000. This condition, which is urgent in consequence of the depressed state of the colonies, we think may easily be complied with, by renouncing the scheme of erecting a new story above the hall in the governmenthouse, and by limitiug the works in question, merely to this, that there be put a new roof on the building containing the governmenthall, and that the inside arrangements undergo the needful restoration. When thus limited, we think that the cost of the whole work to be done will be within $6000. (To be continued.)

From the London Times. When the first Embassy departed from these shores to the unknown city of Pekin the expedition created almost as much sensation as would have been occasioned hy a voyage to the moon. We are now despatching an Ambassador to t lie same country under very different conditions; hut it happens that at this moment an Embassy is on its way, pro-

bably to London, which is at least as extraordinary as the first British mission to China. Never from the earliest periods of history has a diplomatic mission been sent out from the Empire of Japan until the present day; hut now nearly a hundred Japanese have started on what is likely to he a tour of the world, and perhaps before the London season is over we may see genuine specimens of this wonderful people in the Crystal Palace or on the hanks of the Serpentine. The prospect is due to the Americans, who have got the first visit for themselves, and who, as even their official publications show, are not a little pleased at their success. When the treaty of amity between the Americans and the Japanese had been followed by a commercial treaty, it was agreed that the ratifications of the latter instrument should he exchanged in the city ol Washington, an understanding which necessarily involved the appearance of a Japanese Envoy at the American capital. Shortly afterwards the Government of Japan applied to .Mr. Harris, the American Consul-General at Simoda, for a vessel of war in which the proposed Embassy might make the voyage, seeing that the Emperor had no ship fit to cross the Pacific, while the ordinary passenger steamers would not afford agreeable means of conveyance. This request was promptly communicated hy Mr. Harris to the Ann rican Secretary of State at Washington, and favourably received; in fact, tbe Embassy would have started a I we I ve-month sooner hut for a remarkable impediment.
